entries.question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude that Analia ends up controlling Corrupted Conscience (and Lay Claim) and thus gains control of Bane Alley Blackguard.
entries.answer:
After Analia's Lay Claim resolves, Analia controls all three permanents: Lay Claim, Corrupted Conscience, and Analia's Bane Alley Blackguard.

Why: Lay Claim reads "Enchant permanent / You control enchanted permanent," and Corrupted Conscience is itself a permanent (an Aura enchantment), so it's a legal target. Once Lay Claim is attached, Analia becomes the controller of Corrupted Conscience — an Aura's controller is tracked separately from what it's attached to (rule 303.4e).

Corrupted Conscience says "You control enchanted creature." The word "you" on an Aura means that Aura's controller, which is now Analia. Control-changing effects are all applied together in layer 2 (rule 613.1b), and within that layer the effect of Corrupted Conscience now grants control to Analia rather than Nico. So Bane Alley Blackguard goes back to Analia — who also happens to be its owner and its default controller (rule 110.2). Nico keeps nothing from this arrangement.

Note the general principle in the Lay Claim ruling: gaining control of a creature does not give you the Auras on it, and an Aura's "you" always refers to the Aura's own controller. Here Analia used that principle in reverse — instead of taking the creature, she took the Aura that grants control of the creature, and the creature followed.

Bane Alley Blackguard remains enchanted by Corrupted Conscience, so it still has infect. This works the same whether the game has exactly two players or more; no multiplayer-specific rule changes the outcome (control questions would only shift if a player left the game, per rule 800.4a).

entries.answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. However, the effects from both auras apply in the same layer, applying the Lay Claim's effect would change how the Corrupted Conscience's effect is applied, and applying the Corrupted Conscience's effect would not change how the Lay Claim's effect is applied, so the Corrupted Conscience's effect is dependent on the Lay Claim's effect. The Lay Claim's effect applies first, giving Analia control of Corrupted Conscience, and then the Corrupted Conscience's effect applies, giving Analia control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

entries.question: Alan controls [Iroas, God of Victory] and 3 other enchantments. Their devotion to white is 2. They cast [Starfield of Nyx]. After it resolves, is Iroas, God of Victory a creature? If so, what are its power and toughness?

entries.answer:
Yes — after Starfield of Nyx resolves, Iroas, God of Victory is a creature, and it's a 4/4.

Why:

1. Enchantment count: Alan controls Iroas, God of Victory, 3 other enchantments, and Starfield of Nyx itself = five enchantments, so Starfield of Nyx's ability is active. Iroas, God of Victory is a non-Aura enchantment other than Starfield of Nyx, so it's affected.

2. Type-changing (layer 4): Iroas, God of Victory's own ability says "As long as your devotion to red and white is less than seven, Iroas isn't a creature." Devotion to red and white counts every red and/or white mana symbol among the mana costs of permanents Alan controls [700.5a]; with devotion to white only 2, the combined total is well under seven, so that ability is trying to remove the creature type. Starfield of Nyx says the enchantment "is a creature in addition to its other types." Both effects apply in layer 4, and within a layer effects apply in timestamp order [613.1, 613.6, 613.4a]. Starfield of Nyx entered the battlefield later, so its effect is applied after Iroas, God of Victory's, and the final result is that Iroas, God of Victory is a creature (an enchantment creature).

3. Power/toughness (layer 7b): Starfield of Nyx sets "base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value." Iroas, God of Victory's mana cost is {2}{R}{W}, mana value 4, so its base power and toughness become 4/4, replacing the printed 7/4 [302.4c, 613.1g, 613.4a]. With no other pump effects, counters, or anchor-word effects mentioned, it's a 4/4 indestructible Legendary Enchantment Creature — God.

Timing note: I'm assuming Starfield of Nyx has the later timestamp (it just entered). If instead an effect gave Iroas, God of Victory's non-creature ability a later timestamp, it would be applied after Starfield of Nyx and Iroas, God of Victory would not be a creature — though the layer-7b power/toughness setting effect would still exist and simply do nothing while it isn't a creature [208.3a].

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes with player count; devotion only counts permanents Alan controls.

Iroas, God of Victory is a creature with power and toughness equal to its mana value.

In the type layer, there are 2 effects that impact Iroas, God of Victory's type. They are applied in timestamp order, so first Iroas, God of Victory's effect causes Iroas, God of Victory to not be a creature, then Starfield of Nyx's ability causes Iroas, God of Victory to become a creature.

That matters because replacement/prevention-style and damage-result effects are not locked in ahead of time — they're checked as the damage event happens [614.1] [615.1] [120.4b] [120.4c]. Belt and suspenders: even if Inkmoth Nexus had kept infect, Melira, Sylvok Outcast's "You can't get poison counters" would stop the poison counter, and Nadia would simply not lose life either — the damage would have no result at all, though damage-triggered abilities would still see it [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1] [702.90b].

At that point the equipped creature has protection from blue from a blue Equipment, so 702.16d's state-based action (704.1 — state-based actions happen automatically and don't use the stack) unattaches Sword of Body and Mind, which stays on the battlefield. If instead Autumn tries to activate equip after Gift of Tusks has already worn off, the ability can still be activated and resolve, but Sword of Body and Mind will immediately fall off the same way.

Also note the general precedence rule: if some other effect said Painter's Servant "can't be equipped," that "can't" would win (101.2a) — but no such effect is present here. 4. With Murmuring Bosk being a Mountain and not a Forest (and not a Saproling), Life and Limb has nothing to apply to, so Murmuring Bosk is not a 1/1 green Saproling creature. entries.question: April casts [Spontaneous Flight] targeting their [Mist Dragon]. After that resolves April then activates its 'lose flying' ability. Finale of Devastation's ruling confirms the creature you just put onto the battlefield does get +X/+X and haste when X is 10 or more, and that no player can act in between [Finale of Devastation ruling #2, Finale of Devastation ruling #0].

Timing caveat: if instead Humility entered the battlefield *after* Finale of Devastation resolved (later timestamp), Humility's ability-removal would apply after the haste grant and the creature would lose haste — though it would still be 11/11, since Humility only sets base power/toughness in layer 7b while the +10/+10 applies in layer 7c [Humility ruling #2].

entries.question:
Alison controls [Mycosynth Lattice], an [Animate Dead] attached to a [Great-Horn Krushok] that it returned to the battlefield, a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that copied [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] with its second ability, and a [Southern Elephant] enchanted by a [Deep Freeze].

Alison casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield. Alison then puts [Sculpting Steel] onto the battlefield, choosing to copy the Mizzium Transreliquat and then choosing to copy the Animate Dead with its new copy ability. They choose to enchant a [Gigantosaurus] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines.

After Sculpting Steel's trigger resolves and returns the Gigantosaurus to the battlefield, Alison activates the ability of the Sculpting Steel to turn it into a copy of Deep Freeze. After that resolves, they casts [Enchantment Alteration] to attach it to the Southern Elephant. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Sculpting Steel becomes a Deep Freeze attached to Southern Elephant (and loses the Animate Dead leave-the-battlefield sacrifice effect), whereas the reference says Sculpting Steel still has the "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with Animate Dead" condition and does not become attached to Southern Elephant.
entries.answer:
Bottom line: the Sculpting Steel ends up as a permanent copy of Deep Freeze (still carrying Mizzium Transreliquat's {1}{U}{R} copy ability) attached to Southern Elephant, Southern Elephant is a 0/4 blue Wall artifact creature with defender and no other abilities, and Gigantosaurus stays on the battlefield as a normal 10/10 (artifact, via Mycosynth Lattice) and is NOT sacrificed.

Step by step:

1. Sculpting Steel entering. Sculpting Steel's replacement effect copies Mizzium Transreliquat. Because Mizzium Transreliquat had used its second ability, its copiable values are those of Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus the granted "{1}{U}{R}: ...except it has this ability" (707.9a, 613.1a, Sculpting Steel ruling #4, Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #3, Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #0). That includes Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' own "enter as a copy of another creature you control" replacement effect, so Alison applies a second copy effect and Sculpting Steel enters as a copy of Animate Dead. Animate Dead was a legal choice only because Mycosynth Lattice made it an artifact and March of the Machines made that noncreature artifact into a creature at that moment.

2. Timing assumption: March of the Machines was sacrificed to Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked later in the same resolution of Eureka, before any player would receive priority. That matters, because while March of the Machines and Mycosynth Lattice are both out, an Aura that is also a creature can't enchant anything and would be unattached and then put into its owner's graveyard as state-based actions (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3). Since state-based actions aren't checked mid-resolution, and March of the Machines is gone by the time Eureka finishes, both Animate Dead and the new Aura survive attached. If instead March of the Machines had still been on the battlefield when priority came back, every Aura here (Animate Dead, Deep Freeze, and the Sculpting Steel copy) would have been unattached and put into its owner's graveyard.

3. The copied Animate Dead trigger resolves, returning Gigantosaurus to the battlefield and attaching Sculpting Steel (as Animate Dead) to it; Gigantosaurus is 9/10 from the -1/-0 at that point.

4. Activating the {1}{U}{R} ability targeting Deep Freeze. Deep Freeze is a legal target because Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts. Sculpting Steel becomes a copy of Deep Freeze, except it keeps that copy ability. This change happens while it stays on the battlefield, so no enters/leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger and non-copy effects continue (707.4). Crucially, it no longer has Animate Dead's "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" ability — the copy effect overwrote its text. Its enchant ability is now "enchant creature," and Gigantosaurus is a creature, so it remains legally attached. Because this came from the second (non-"until end of turn") ability, it does not wear off at end of turn (Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #2). Gigantosaurus becomes base 0/4, a blue Wall with defender, and loses all other abilities.

5. Enchantment Alteration moves the Aura from Gigantosaurus (a creature) to Southern Elephant (another creature), which is legal, and the Aura gets a new timestamp (701.3c). Gigantosaurus is left unenchanted: back to 10/10 Dinosaur (still an artifact from Mycosynth Lattice) and it is not sacrificed, since the Animate Dead sacrifice ability no longer exists anywhere.

6. Southern Elephant now has two Deep Freeze effects on it (the original Deep Freeze and the copy). The later-timestamped one overwrites the earlier base-P/T setting, but they set the same values (Deep Freeze ruling #2), so Southern Elephant is a 0/4 blue Wall (plus artifact from Mycosynth Lattice) with defender and no other abilities.

Player count: nothing here changes between two players and multiplayer, except that Eureka lets every player put permanents onto the battlefield and simultaneous choices would be made in APNAP order (101.4); with more opponents, more permanents could enter during that resolution.

entries.question: Alex controls [Karametra, God of Harvests], and then casts [Opalescence]. Their devotion to white is 2. Is Karametra, God of Harvests a creature? If so, what is its power and toughness?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Opalescence's later type-changing effect makes Karametra a creature and Opalescence sets its power and toughness to its mana value (5/5).
entries.answer:
Yes — Karametra, God of Harvests is a creature, and it's 5/5.

Why: Both Karametra, God of Harvests' own ability ("As long as your devotion to green and white is less than seven, Karametra isn't a creature") and Opalescence's ability ("Each other non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types...") are type-changing continuous effects, so both apply in layer 4, in timestamp order (rules 613.1, 613.7, and see Opalescence ruling #3, which confirms the type change happens in layer 4 and the base power/toughness setting happens later, in layer 7b).

Devotion here is low: devotion to green and white counts green and/or white mana symbols in the mana costs of permanents you control (rule 700.5a). Karametra, God of Harvests' cost {3}{G}{W} contributes 2 ({G} and {W}; the {3} is generic and doesn't count), and Opalescence's cost {2}{W}{W} contributes 2. So with just these permanents, devotion to green and white is 4, which is less than seven — Karametra, God of Harvests' own ability would strip its creature type (Karametra ruling #15).

But Opalescence entered later, so its layer‑4 effect is applied after Karametra, God of Harvests' effect and makes Karametra, God of Harvests a creature (in addition to being a legendary enchantment). Then in layer 7b Opalescence sets its base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value; Karametra, God of Harvests' mana value is 5 ({3}{G}{W}), so it is 5/5 — not its printed 6/7, because a base-P/T-setting effect overrides the printed values (rules 208.4b, 208.1, and the Base Power/Base Toughness glossary entry).

Timing note: this answer assumes Karametra, God of Harvests has the earlier timestamp (it was already on the battlefield, as stated). If Opalescence had the earlier timestamp, Karametra, God of Harvests' own ability would be applied last in layer 4 and it would not be a creature (and, having no creature type, would have no power or toughness per rules 208.3 and 302.4) — though Opalescence would still set base P/T in layer 7b, that's irrelevant while it isn't a creature.

Nothing here depends on player count; devotion and layers work the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Karametra, God of Harvests is a creature with power and toughness equal to its mana value.

In the type layer, there are 2 effects that impact Karametra, God of Harvests's type. They are applied in timestamp order, so first Karametra, God of Harvests's effect causes Karametra, God of Harvests to not be a creature, then Opalescence's ability causes Karametra, God of Harvests to become a creature.

entries.question: Autumn animates [Inkmoth Nexus] and attacks with it. Nayeli then flashes in [Dress Down]. What does Inkmoth Nexus look like?

entries.question: Aaron equips [Skullclamp] onto [Champion of the Flame]. Does Champion of the Flame die?

entries.question: In their first main phase, Alexandra activates [Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance] to create two tokens, and Nehemiah responds with [Dress Down]. What happens with the tokens?

entries.answer:
The two tokens are still created, and they still have haste. Nehemiah's Dress Down doesn't stop tokens from being created and doesn't strip the haste in this case.

Why: Alexandra's Channel ability from Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance is already on the stack when Nehemiah casts Dress Down with flash, so Dress Down is on top and resolves first (rule 608.1). Dress Down then sets up its continuous "Creatures lose all abilities" effect. Nothing about Dress Down says a permanent with those characteristics can't enter the battlefield, so rule 111.5 (the only rule that stops token creation for that reason) doesn't apply — the tokens exist.

The haste survives because the same resolution of Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance's ability grants haste after Dress Down is already on the battlefield. Per Dress Down ruling #0, an ability granted to a creature after Dress Down has entered isn't lost; Dress Down only removes abilities the creature already had. The Spirit tokens have no printed abilities of their own to lose, so the net result is two 1/1 colorless Spirits with haste that can attack this turn.

Assumed timing: Nehemiah cast Dress Down in response to the activated ability, so Dress Down resolves first. If instead Dress Down had somehow already resolved and then the tokens were created — that's the same outcome here. The only case where the tokens would lose haste is if the haste grant happened before Dress Down entered the battlefield (i.e., Dress Down cast after the Channel ability fully resolved); then the tokens would lose haste, though they'd remain on the battlefield as 1/1 Spirits.

Dress Down also triggers its own "draw a card" for Nehemiah, and it is sacrificed at the beginning of the end step; the tokens remain on the battlefield after that (they only cease to exist if they leave the battlefield, per rules 111.7 and 704.5d). None of this depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

entries.question: Niko controls [Urza's Saga] on chapter 2. Ainsley casts [Magus of the Moon]. What happens to Urza's Saga?

entries.answer:

Why: Magus of the Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." That sacrifice is a state-based action, so it happens as soon as a player would receive priority and doesn't use the stack [704.5s], [714.4].

entries.question: Ariana controls [Painter's Servant] naming "blue." Nico casts [Dress Down]. What color are Painter's Servant and Dress Down?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Painter's Servant becomes colorless after Dress Down, whereas the correct ruling is that the Servant's color-changing ability already applied (layer 5) so both permanents are blue.
entries.answer:
After Dress Down resolves: Painter's Servant is colorless, and Dress Down is blue.

Why:

1. Dress Down says "Creatures lose all abilities." Painter's Servant is an Artifact Creature — Scarecrow, so it loses both "As this creature enters, choose a color" and the static ability "All cards that aren't on the battlefield, spells, and permanents are the chosen color in addition to their other colors." With that static ability gone, nothing is adding blue to anything anymore.

2. Painter's Servant's mana cost is {2} — entirely generic mana, no colored symbols — so by rule 202.2a an object with a mana cost of {2} is colorless, and it has no color indicator (204.2) or color-defining characteristic-defining ability (105.2, 604.3) left to change that. So Painter's Servant is colorless.

3. Dress Down's mana cost is {1}{U}: one generic mana plus one blue mana. The {U} makes it blue (202.2a, 202.2f), and Dress Down doesn't remove its own or any enchantment's abilities, only creatures'. So Dress Down is mono-blue.

Timing note: I'm assuming you're asking about the state after Dress Down has resolved. Before that — while Dress Down is still a spell on the stack — Painter's Servant's ability is intact, so it applies to spells and permanents: Painter's Servant itself would be blue (a normally colorless object simply becomes the chosen color rather than being blue and colorless, per Painter's Servant ruling #0), and Dress Down would be blue in addition to its other colors, which is still just blue since blue was chosen (Painter's Servant ruling #5). So the visible change on resolution is only to Painter's Servant, which goes from blue to colorless.

Also note that a genuine color-changing effect would overwrite Painter's Servant's added color (105.3, 613.1e layer 5, Painter's Servant ruling #4), but Dress Down isn't such an effect — it works by stripping the ability itself.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on player count, and Painter's Servant affects all cards, spells, and permanents regardless of controller.

entries.question: Anabella controls [Blood Moon] and enchants their [Sunlit Marsh] with [Urban Utopia]. What colors can it tap for?

entries.answer:
Sunlit Marsh can tap for any one color — white, blue, black, red, or green — using the ability granted by Urban Utopia, and it also has "{T}: Add {R}" from Blood Moon. What it can no longer do is produce {W} or {B} from its own printed Plains Swamp typeline abilities, because Blood Moon stripped those.

Blood Moon ruling #2: it loses its other land types (Plains, Swamp) and all its abilities, becomes a Mountain, and gains "{T}: Add {R}" — the Mountain type intrinsically grants that ability anyway ([Mountain], [305.6]).
- Urban Utopia grants the enchanted land "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Since the Aura was put onto Sunlit Marsh after Blood Moon was already applying (the timing I'm assuming from the question's order), its ability-granting effect has the later timestamp and is applied after Blood Moon's ability-removal, so the granted mana ability sticks. Urban Utopia ruling #0 also confirms Urban Utopia doesn't change the land's types, so Sunlit Marsh stays a Mountain.
- "Any color" means one of the five colors: white, blue, black, red, or green ([105.1], [107.4a]). Each activation produces one mana of a single color you choose; it is not colorless mana ({C}) and not generic.

Timing caveat: if instead Urban Utopia had been attached first and Blood Moon entered afterward, Blood Moon's later timestamp would remove the granted "{T}: Add one mana of any color" ability too, leaving Sunlit Marsh able to produce only {R}.

Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

entries.question: What layer does [Grand Abolisher]'s "During your turn, your opponents can't cast spells or activate abilities of artifacts, creatures, or enchantments." ability apply in?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Grand Abolisher's ability does not apply in any layer but is a static ability producing a continuous rule-prohibiting effect, and it matches the reference's scope clarifications.
entries.answer:
Grand Abolisher's ability doesn't apply in any of the layers at all. The layer system of rule 613 exists only to determine the values of an object's characteristics — continuous effects that change copiable values (layer 1), control (layer 2), abilities (layer 6), and so on [613.1, 613.1a, 613.1b, 613.1f]. Grand Abolisher's ability changes no characteristic of any object; it is a static ability that generates a continuous effect stating that something can't happen (your opponents can't cast spells or activate abilities of artifacts, creatures, or enchantments during your turn). Effects that say something can't happen aren't characteristic-modifying effects and aren't replacement effects either; they simply prohibit the action [614.17], and a player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated [602.5].

So there's no timestamp or dependency question to resolve for Grand Abolisher within a layer [613.3, 613.7, 613.8] — it just applies as a restriction whenever an opponent tries to cast a spell or activate a qualifying ability during your turn.

Two notes on scope from the card's own rulings: Grand Abolisher does not stop triggered or static abilities [Grand Abolisher ruling #0], and it does not stop activated abilities of artifact, creature, or enchantment cards in zones other than the battlefield, such as cycling from hand [Grand Abolisher ruling #1].

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games: the card says "your opponents," so at a multiplayer table it restricts every opponent, not just one, during each of your turns.

entries.answer_gold: Because Grand Abolisher's ability doesn't change the characteristics of any objects, it doesn't apply in any layer. Instead it's a static ability that generates a continuous effect that modifies the rules of the game.
